transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Sara Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Zoe Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (NexaDocs HoML), Jon Reyes (NexaDocs Platform), Ethan Wu (NexaDocs CTO), Maya Singh (NexaDocs Security)

Summary:
A technical deep dive focused on long-context (128k+ tokens) performance: chunking strategies, KV cache behavior, continuous cache, batching tradeoffs, attention optimizations, quantization impact, and deployment options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs VPC/on-prem). Action items and next steps captured at top.

Topics covered:
- Long context handling (128k+) and memory/IO implications
- Chunking and overlap strategies for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and note-taking flows
- KV cache management, warmup, and cross-request reuse
- Batching and latency-throughput tradeoffs at 1k-10k QPS
- Attention kernel optimizations (sparse, flash attention variants) and their real-world impact
- Quantization profiles (4-bit/8-bit) and accuracy vs perf tradeoffs
- VPC/on-prem constraints: network, KMS, audit logs, and cold start implications

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Sara (Redwood): all right everyone thanks for joining. we'll kick off — agenda is long-context perf, want to cover chunking, kv cache, kernel choices, and then deployment options. quick intros?
[00:00:12] Priya (NexaDocs): hi this is priya, head of ml at nexa docs. we're building a doc understanding product, lots of long documents, wanting 128k+ context for multi-document synthesis.
[00:00:22] Ethan (NexaDocs): ethan here, CTO, mainly interested in perf and cost.
[00:00:26] Sara: cool. liam you're gonna lead tech deep-dive?
[00:00:29] Liam (Redwood): yeah thanks. quick note, transcription may have weird names, sorry for any typos. so first, can you give a couple of representative workloads and qps?
[00:00:40] Priya: typical user flow — ingest 10-50 long docs per case, we do retrieval and chunking, then a 10-20k token prompt to synthesize. peak queries maybe 200-400 QPS for search while inference QPS is lower, like 20-40 qps; but offline batch jobs could spike. experimenting with single-shot giant context where we want the model to see entire 128k for some usecases.
[00:01:05] Liam: got it. so we're looking at two orthogonal problems: memory and compute for single 128k attention, and system design for streaming/chunked pipelines.

[00:01:18] Zoe (Redwood): quick perf numbers from our infra: on A100-class nodes, a full 128k forward+decode with native attention is extremely expensive — tens to hundreds of GBs of intermediate memory depending on head dims. we typically advocate chunking with overlap and a KV caching strategy for autoregressive decodes.
[00:01:36] Jon (NexaDocs): when you say chunking with overlap, how much overlap do you recommend? we worry about hallucinations at chunk boundaries.
[00:01:45] Liam: good q. rule of thumb: overlap window about 256-1024 tokens depending on coherence needs. for summarization tasks heavier overlap reduces boundary artifacts. critical to include chunk metadata and position embeddings so the model knows relative ordering.

[00:02:05] Priya: do you use sliding windows or hierarchical chunking? we have hierarchical retrieval in place.
[00:02:11] Liam: both patterns are valid. for 128k contexts, hierarchical retrieval => coarse filter then fine-grained chunks fed into the model is common. sliding-window is simpler and can work for extracts. we also support streaming the KV cache so earlier chunks don't need to be re-encoded each time if you maintain a persistent cache per session.

[00:02:30] Sara: let's dig into KV cache — Liam, can you explain continuous KV cache and warmup behavior?
[00:02:35] Liam: sure. continuous KV cache means we keep key/value tensors for previous tokens in GPU memory and reuse them across requests for the same session. warmup happens when session is cold; first N tokens need compute to populate cache. if you have many short requests, the cache reuse ratio drops and per-token CPU/GPU overhead increases. for 128k, the cache is large — we shard it across GPUs or use spill-to-CPU if needed, but spills hurt latency.
[00:03:02] Ethan: spill-to-disk not acceptable for latency SLOs. what are the typical memory footprints?
[00:03:08] Zoe: approximate: for a 30B model, KV per token might be 64-128 bytes per head per layer; ballpark a 128k context could produce multiple GBs per shard — we usually recommend model quantization plus shard-aware routing to keep it in GPU. for really long contexts we advise either Dedicated pools with larger GPU memory (80GB+ per host) or model variants optimized for long context (sparsified attention).

[00:03:34] Priya: so in practice for our hosted usage, would Dedicated be needed? we prefer hosted but worried about cost buckets.
[00:03:42] Sara: depends on your SLOs. Hosted can handle batchy/streamed workloads with our routing but sustained low-latency 128k sessions at scale typically map to Dedicated/reserved capacity where you can guarantee GPU memory and pin nodes. Redwood Dedicated offers guaranteed shard placements and autoscale policies.
[00:03:59] Jon: what about VPC on-prem? our security team leans that direction.
[00:04:03] Liam: VPC/private deployment supports the same runtime but you manage networking and KMS. on-prem adds operational overhead: node provisioning, NUMA considerations, and cold-start times. we provide a private control plane and KMS integrations but some kernels require specific CUDA/cuDNN versions on premises.

[00:04:20] Maya (NexaDocs): security: can we audit KV cache eviction events and encryption at rest for cached tensors?
[00:04:27] Sara: yes we can log cache lifecycle events to audit logs. encryption at-rest is supported for persistent spills and model artifacts via KMS/HSM; in-host GPU memory is ephemeral and handled by access controls. we'll include more details in the security pack.

[00:04:42] Liam: switching to attention kernels — there are several optimized implementations: flash attention variants, chunked-linear attention, and sparse attention for long sequences. flash attention reduces memory by computing attention in tiles and is great for GPUs with ample shared memory. sparse attention (BigBird/Longformer style) reduces asymptotic cost but can impact model compatibility; many open checkpoints are finetuned with sparse-aware patterns.
[00:05:06] Priya: do you recommend re-training or fine-tuning models to accept sparse patterns?
[00:05:11] Liam: if you need native sparse attention for cost reasons, re-tuning is recommended but not always required — you can use approximations like chunked attention with global tokens. tradeoff is accuracy vs cost. we often run A/B evals on held-out prompts to measure regression.

[00:05:26] Jon: quantization — what level is safe for long-context retrieval?
[00:05:30] Zoe: we usually test 8-bit first; 4-bit (GPTQ/QnA-style) gives bigger memory wins but sometimes introduces subtle tokenization/formatting errors, especially on long-coherence tasks. for RAG pipelines, 8-bit is often a sweet spot. we can provide quality/latency matrices per model.

[00:05:44] Priya: any tips on batching? our infra does variable-length prompts.
[00:05:49] Liam: batch size tuning: larger batches increase throughput but add queueing latency. for low-latency interactive flows you want small batches (1-4) plus adaptive batching where we pad to similar length. for throughput-heavy offline inference, push larger batches and use micro-batching inside the runtime. Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching and dynamic padding strategies.

[00:06:08] Ethan: can you share concrete numbers — e.g., latency for a 128k encoding pass vs chunked 8k windows?
[00:06:15] Zoe: approximate numbers (very workload dependent): single 128k attention forward can be 50-300s on a single A100 if done naively; chunked approach with 16 x 8k windows plus overlap and cached encodings can bring end-to-end down to 6-20s depending on decode length. that's why chunking + cache is the practical pattern.
[00:06:38] Priya: wow big difference. so for real-time product we probably need chunk+cache.

[00:06:44] Liam: yes. also pre-encode static documents offline and persist embeddings/KV snapshots for fast session assembly. that reduces warmup considerably.

[00:06:55] Jon: how does Redwood handle fallback if Dedicated capacity is saturated?
[00:06:59] Sara: policy-based routing: requests can failover to compatible model variants in hosted pool (smaller quantized model) or queue with backpressure. for latency-sensitive flows we recommend multi-tier capacity planning.

[00:07:09] Priya: any guidance on cost per 128k query? even rough order-of-magnitude helps procurement.
[00:07:15] Sara: cost varies a lot. ballpark: naive full-attention 128k on large model — very expensive — thousands per request in infra. chunked+cache decreases cost by 5-50x depending on reuse. we'll provide a cost model spreadsheet based on your expected reuse/throughput.

[00:07:31] Liam: a couple of gotchas we've seen: 1) unbounded session lifetimes can blow up memory due to KV retention; add TTL or LRU eviction policies per session. 2) careful with shard placement — cross-GPU KV fetches add network latency. colocate shards when possible. 3) for on-prem, PCIe vs NVLink topology matters a lot for KV movement.

[00:07:55] Zoe: also watch evaluation metrics. long-context tasks need prompt-level evals for coherence; token-level perplexity doesn't capture hallucination in multi-doc synthesis.

[00:08:05] Priya: about chunk metadata — you mentioned position embeddings — we're currently concatenating chunk ids in prompts, is there a better pattern?
[00:08:12] Liam: yes include structured prefix like [DOC 3: offset 1200-8000] metadata and use template instructions. some teams embed chunk vectors and rely on cross-attention to retrieve; others append a small textual descriptor. The key is consistent ordering and allowing the model to know boundaries.

[00:08:30] Ethan: on the tooling side, can we get tracing for token-level latency and per-shard kernel breakdown?
[00:08:35] Sara: Redwood Console provides per-route token latency, model breakdown, and trace hooks. for Dedicated/Private we can expose more granular traces and raw perf logs for benchmarking. we'll attach sample traces to the benchmark runbook.

[00:08:49] Jon: for the pilot, we want to run end-to-end with our sample corpus. what's the recommended setup?
[00:08:54] Liam: recommended: 1) provide representative corpus and query patterns, 2) choose a model candidate (we'll suggest two variants: quantized 8-bit 30B and a 70B 4-bit variant for comparison), 3) Redwood runs bench with chunking strategies (sliding vs hierarchical) and KV cache configs, 4) analyze latency/throughput and regression on quality metrics. we'll share raw logs and consolidated reports.

[00:09:20] Priya: any notes on attention recomputation to save memory?
[00:09:24] Zoe: attention recomputation (checkpointing) trades compute for memory; good when memory is the constraint but increases runtime. combined with quantization it can be viable. we often mix recomputation with Flash kernels to balance memory footprint.

[00:09:36] Ethan: are there production customers doing 128k+ right now?
[00:09:40] Sara: yes, a handful in enterprise verticals for legal and pharma. patterns are consistent: heavy offline pre-encode, persistent KV snapshots, dedicated capacity for hotspots, and careful eviction policies.

[00:09:52] Jon: how will model updates and rollouts affect cached KV? if we update model, do we need to invalidate KV caches?
[00:09:59] Liam: good point — caches are model-specific; changing base model or tokenization can invalidate caches. we support versioned caches and rollouts where we warm new caches gradually while keeping a fallback to old model until warmup thresholds are met.

[00:10:12] Priya: okay looks like next steps are clear. can you share benchmark runbook and security docs?
[00:10:18] Sara: yes, action items summarized earlier. we will share the runbook, cost model, and security pack.

[00:10:24] Ethan: one quick practical question — for debugging, can we get raw kernel timing breakdowns?
[00:10:28] Zoe: yes for Dedicated/Private we can surface kernel-level timings and NVLink transfer times; for Hosted we provide aggregated traces but can run deeper lab runs on request.

[00:10:38] Priya: any final gotchas about multi-tenant hosted impl?
[00:10:42] Liam: multi-tenant adds noisy-neighbor variability; we mitigate with isolation classes and jitterless scheduling but for strict SLOs Dedicated is better.

[00:10:50] Sara: great. we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the pilot kickoff. thanks everyone.

[00:10:55] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: there are occasional mis-hearings, product names like "Redwood Dedicated" were sometimes transcribed as "Redwood Dedicate" or "Redwood Dedicat", and some technical terms (e.g., NVLink, FlashAttention) were tokenized inconsistently.
